titleText.es: Sus libros intimidaban bastante; descolgarme por su tragaluz me pareció la mejor opción.
titleText.en: His books were fairly intimidating; climbing down through his skylight seemed like the best option.
titleText.noteEn: The title text extends the joke by explaining how the speaker entered Knuth's house.

regions.labelEs: TÍO, ERES MUY INCONSISTENTE CON LOS ÍNDICES DE TUS ARRAYS. A VECES EMPIEZAN EN UNO Y OTRAS EN CERO.

applications.explanationEn: A and veces form the fixed frequency expression a veces.

regions.labelEs: DIFERENTES TAREAS EXIGEN DIFERENTES CONVENCIONES. CITANDO AL EXPERTO EN ALGORÍTMICA DE STANFORD, DONALD KNUTH, ¿QUIÉN ERES TÚ? ¿CÓMO HAS ENTRADO EN MI CASA?

applications.explanationEn: Al combines the personal a with el before the specific person experto.
Quién directly asks which person, so it carries a written accent.
Eres already signals “you,” while tú makes the unknown person's identity emphatic.
Cómo asks about the manner in which something happened, so it carries a written accent.
Has is the present form of haber for tú, and entrado is the unchanged participle that follows it.
Cómo is a direct question here, so it keeps its written accent.

regions.labelEs: BUENO, ESO FUE LO QUE DIJO CUANDO LE PREGUNTÉ AL RESPECTO.

applications.explanationEn: Bueno delays and softens the speaker's explanation rather than describing something as good.
Lo que points to the unnamed content of what Knuth said.
Al respecto points back to the matter that was just quoted.

cards.noteEn: Tío literally means “uncle,” but in casual speech in Spain it can address a male friend much like “dude” or “man.”

example.es: Tío, no me lo puedo creer.

cards.promptEs: índices de arrays desde cero o desde uno
cards.answerEn: different systems number an array's first item as either 0 or 1
cards.noteEn: Programming languages and algorithms use indexing conventions to label positions. Mixing zero-based and one-based conventions makes the same index point to different items.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of a veces, “sometimes”

cards.questionEn: How do you say “sometimes” in Spanish?
cards.noteEn: This common time expression describes something that happens on some occasions but not always. It normally sits before or after the verb without changing form.
In frequency expressions such as a veces and algunas veces, English commonly translates the whole expression as “sometimes.”

cards.answerEn: a + el before a specific person; often “the” or “to the” in English
cards.noteEn: Spanish contracts a + el to al. The personal a can mark a specific person who receives or is affected by an action; English may use “the,” “to the,” or no separate preposition, depending on the verb.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.

cards.answerEn: an influential computer scientist and author of The Art of Computer Programming
cards.noteEn: Knuth taught at Stanford and is a natural authority to cite about algorithms and programming conventions.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?
Why might Spanish say tú or yo when the verb already tells you who acts?
cards.answerEn: Say the subject pronoun to add emphasis, contrast, or clarity; otherwise Spanish often leaves it out.
cards.noteEn: A verb form such as eres already points to “you.” Adding tú can stress that particular person, especially in a contrast or a surprised question. The pronoun may appear after the verb.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.answerEn: entered; come in (past participle of entrar)
It can mean “well…,” giving the speaker time or softening the reply.
cards.noteEn: Here bueno organizes the conversation rather than describing a person or thing. A pause after it can signal hesitation, reluctance, or a gentle correction.
cards.questionEn: What can bueno mean at the start of an answer when it is not describing something as good?

cards.answerEn: was (a completed past instance of ser)
what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Lo combines with que to refer to an idea, action, or whole situation rather than a masculine noun. Together, lo que means “what” or “the thing that.”

cards.questionEn: How do you say “what” or “the thing that” without naming a specific object?
cards.answerEn: Use lo que to refer to an idea, action, situation, or unnamed thing.
cards.noteEn: Here lo is neutral: it does not stand for a masculine noun. Que introduces the information that identifies the idea or thing. Together they work as one unit.

example.en: I don't understand what you're saying.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Here que completes lo que, a neutral expression meaning “what” or “the thing that.” It does not refer to a particular masculine or feminine noun.

Le usually marks an indirect object, such as a recipient (“to him”). With a masculine person, especially in Spain, le can also be used as the direct object (“him”); this accepted use is called leísmo.

example.es: Le di el libro a Pablo.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of al respecto, “about it”

cards.questionEn: How do you refer back to a topic as “about it” or “on that matter”?
cards.noteEn: This expression points back to a matter already being discussed. Al is part of the fixed expression and does not need to name a masculine noun after it.

example.es: No tengo más preguntas al respecto.
example.en: I have no more questions about it.
